extracted.intended_audience: graduate/advanced undergraduate students studying algebraic geometry (Math 216 / readers of Vakil)
extracted.subtask_description: Textbook exposition and exercises on graphs of rational maps, proper morphisms (definitions, examples, stability properties, and consequences), rigidity and abelian varieties, and the notions of dimension and codimension for schemes (including the equality with transcendence degree for finitely generated domains).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph of a rational map (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is reduced and Y is separated, define the graph Γ_π of a rational map π : X ""# Y as follows. Let (U, π') be any representative of this rational map (so π' : U → Y is a morphism). Let Γ_π be the scheme-theoretic closure of Γ_{π'} in X × Y, where the first map is a closed embedding and the second is an open embedding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work in the appropriate category (e.g., k-schemes take fiber product over k). This construction is analogous to graphs of morphisms and yields a canonical closed subscheme of X × Y capturing the rational map; figures and exercises illustrate examples (nonreduced domain, nonseparated target).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence of representative for graph of rational map
rubrics_metrics.description: The graph of a rational map π is independent of the choice of representative of π.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 10.2.E: Hint reduces to the case where one representative domain is the domain of definition of π and asks to show the scheme-theoretic closure of U in X is all of X. (Remark: separatedness of Y is not necessary for this fact.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphs of rational maps can realize blow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain blow-ups arise as graphs of rational maps: e.g., the rational map A^2 -->> P^1 given by (x,y) cannot be extended over the origin, and the graph of this rational map is the morphism described as the blow-up of the plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 10.2.F points to the blow-up construction and indicates that many blow-ups are graphs of rational maps; see related exercises (Cremona transformation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maps to a separated scheme extend over an effective Cartier divisor in at most one way
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose X is a Z-scheme and Y is a separated Z-scheme. If D is an effective Cartier divisor on X, then any Z-morphism X \ D → Y can be extended in at most one way to a Z-morphism X → Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 10.2.G: Reduce to the affine case X = Spec A where D is vanishing of t. Show the image of D(t) is all of X and reduce to showing a scheme-theoretic inclusion At ⊂ A. Uses separatedness of Y and local arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associated-to-separated theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Two S-morphisms π and π' from a locally Noetherian scheme U to a separated S-scheme Z that agree on a dense open subset containing the associated points of U are the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 10.2.H hints at extending the Reduced-to-Separated Theorem to schemes with associated points; used to control uniqueness of morphisms determined on dense opens containing associated points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of universally closed
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism of schemes is universally closed if for every morphism Z → Y the base change X ×_Y Z → Z is closed; equivalently, the morphism remains closed under any base change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This strengthens 'closed' so the property is preserved by base change; motivates the notion of properness. Analogy: for certain topological spaces, being universally closed is equivalent to properness (preimages of compact sets are compact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of proper morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π : X → Y is proper if it is separated, of finite type, and universally closed. A scheme X is proper over A if the structure morphism X → Spec A is proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the fundamental notion of 'compactness' in algebraic geometry; details and examples follow (non-examples include A^1_C over Spec C after suitable base change).

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed embeddings are proper
rubrics_metrics.description: Closed embeddings are proper: they are separated, finite type, and remain closed under base change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 10.3.2: Uses that affine morphisms are separated and closed embeddings remain closed after base change. Serves as a basic class of proper morphisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite morphisms are proper
rubrics_metrics.description: Finite morphisms are proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 10.3.3: Finite morphisms are affine (hence separated), finite type, and remain finite (thus closed) after any base change. This gives an immediate class of proper morphisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability properties of proper morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Properness is preserved under: (a) base change; (b) is local on the target; (c) composition; (d) products; (e) if τ is proper and ρ is separated in a commutative diagram X --τ→ Z --ρ→ Y, then any morphism factoring yields properness of the composite as stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 10.3.4 lists these; proofs reduce to the preservation of separatedness, finite type, and universal closedness under fibered products and composition. (e) is an application using closed embeddings and the Cancellation Theorem for proper morphisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projective schemes are proper
rubrics_metrics.description: Projective A-schemes are proper over A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 10.3.5: Structure morphism factors through a closed embedding into P^n_A followed by P^n_A → Spec A. Closed embeddings and compositions of proper morphisms are proper, so it suffices to show P^n_A → Spec A is universally closed (the Fundamental Theorem of Elimination Theory / Theorem 7.4.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable proper schemes are often projective (remark)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is difficult to produce examples of A-schemes that are proper but not projective; over a field, all proper curves are projective and all smooth surfaces are projective, but counterexamples (proper nonprojective) occur in higher dimensions or with singularities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark 10.3.6 lists pointers to examples to be seen later (singular threefold, certain surfaces, Hironaka's example after flatness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy of functions on connected reduced proper k-schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a connected reduced proper k-scheme with k algebraically closed, then Γ(X, O_X) = k; i.e., global regular functions on such an X are constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 10.3.7: Proof sketches mapping X → A^1 and extending to P^1 using properness; image arguments show image must be a point. Compare with maximum principle intuition from complex geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterizations relating finiteness and properness
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism is finite iff it is proper and affine, and iff it is proper and quasi-finite (Theorem 29.6.2 to be proved later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 10.3.8: Partial proofs given earlier; full proof deferred until after Zariski's Main Theorem. Application: quasi-finite morphisms from proper schemes to separated schemes are finite (use Cancellation Theorem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasi-finite + proper ⇒ finite (application)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π : X → Y is quasi-finite and X is proper over Z while Y is separated over Z, then π is finite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given in 10.3.8: use that composition with properness and separatedness yields properness of π, then proper+quasi-finite ⇒ finite (facts to be completed later). Concrete example: certain rational maps P^1 → P^1 given by homogeneous polynomials with no common roots are finite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigidity Lemma (constraints forcing constancy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X, Y, Z be varieties with X proper and geometrically integral (with rational point p), and Y irreducible. Given α : X × Y → Z such that α is constant on X × {q'} for some q', then (a) there is a morphism ψ : Y → Z with α = ψ ∘ pr on some neighbourhood (i.e., α pulled back from Y); (b) if α is also constant on {p} × Y, then α is constant on all of X × Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigidity Lemma 10.3.12 is a key tool used to deduce rigidity/constancy properties for morphisms from proper sources. Proof uses properness of projections, base change, and reduction to fibers where maps are determined by closed points; several exercises (10.3.D, 10.3.E) expand the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for morphisms from abelian varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is an abelian variety and G a group variety, any morphism φ : A → G is the composition of a translation and a homomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corollary 10.3.13: Proof uses the map α(a1,a2) = φ(a1a2)φ(a1)^{-1}φ(a2)^{-1} and applies the Rigidity Lemma to conclude α is constant, which forces φ to be a homomorphism up to translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of abelian variety
rubrics_metrics.description: An abelian variety over a field k is an algebraic group that is geometrically integral and projective (over k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 10.3.11: Analytification over C gives a complex torus C^n/Λ. Examples (elliptic curves) come later; connectedness and projectivity are crucial to later rigidity/commutativity results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of (Krull) dimension for topological spaces and rings
rubrics_metrics.description: Dimension of a topological space X (dim X) is the supremum of lengths of chains of closed irreducible sets (indexing starts at 0). Dimension of a ring is the supremum of lengths of chains of nested prime ideals (Krull dimension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 11.1.1: Dimension is purely topological for schemes (depends only on underlying topological space); conventions include dim ∅ = −∞. For affine schemes, dim Spec A = dim A; nilpotents are ignored (Spec A ≅ Spec A/N(A)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic examples and computations of dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: dim A^1_k = 1; dim Spec Z = 1; dim Spec k = 0; dim Spec k[x]/(x^2) = 0; dim Spec A = dim A (exercise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 11.1.2 and exercises: identify prime ideals to compute Krull dimensions; use homeomorphisms to reduce by nilradical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codimension (height) for irreducible closed subsets and primes
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y ⊂ X is irreducible closed, codim_X Y is the supremum of lengths of increasing chains of irreducible closed subsets starting with Y (indexing starts at 0). For a prime p in a ring A, the codimension of p equals dim A_p (height).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 11.1.4: Avoid using codimension for reducible subsets without care; codim behaves pathologically in some examples. For varieties (Theorem 11.2.9) codimX Y + dim Y = dim X, but this equality can fail in more general schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codimension one primes in a UFD are principal
rubrics_metrics.description: In a unique factorization domain A, all codimension 1 prime ideals are principal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma 11.1.6: Choose a nonzero element in the prime, take an irreducible factor inside the prime; codimension 1 forces equality of ideals. This highlights the special nature of codimension 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nagata example: Noetherian does not imply finite dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist Noetherian rings of infinite Krull dimension (construct S^{-1}A from A = k[x1,x2,...] with a suitable multiplicative set S), so Noetherianity alone does not force finite dimension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 11.1.K gives the construction and steps to prove S^{-1}A is Noetherian yet has infinite dimension; shows pathologies that motivate later finiteness theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noetherian local rings have finite dimension (remark)
rubrics_metrics.description: Noetherian local rings have finite dimension (points of locally Noetherian schemes have finite codimension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 11.1.8 and references: proof requires Krull's Height Theorem (11.3.7) and will be developed later; this fact prevents some pathologies at local points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension = transcendence degree for finitely generated domains
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a finitely generated domain over a field k, then dim Spec A = tr. deg. K(A)/k. Hence for an irreducible k-variety X, dim X = tr. deg. K(X)/k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 11.2.1: This provides a powerful algebraic interpretation of dimension for varieties. Consequences include computing dimension from function fields, Nullstellensatz corollaries, and behavior under dominant morphisms. Proof uses Noether normalization (developed in subsequent sections).
